What is the essential teaching in 'When You Practice on Your Own'?

In 'When You Practice on Your Own', the teaching opens with this observation: *"When I was in France recently, the question was posed, “When you’re practicing on your own, how do you know what level of practice is appropriate for you?”
This was asked by someone who had been trained in one of those traditions where practices are clearly delineated as being elementary, intermediate, or advanced, and where it’s dangerous to take on the advanced practices before you’ve mastered the earlier ones."* The central invitation is to turn one's investigation inward — to verify the Dhamma not as a set of beliefs, but as directly observable reality in one's own body, speech, and mind. As the text teaches, the Dhamma is *akāliko* — ever-present — and *opanayiko* — leading inward — available to be known (*paccattaṁ*) by each practitioner for themselves. There is no need to search elsewhere; the truth is already here.

Why does the preceptor teach the five meditation themes at ordination?

The text explains: *"If you’re an immoral monk, accepting salutations—as when people place their hands palm-to-palm over the heart: “Which would be better, receiving that kind of salutation, or getting stabbed in the chest with an iron spike?” Again, the monks said, “Ah, the salutation would be better.” But the Buddha said, “If you’re an immoral monk, you’d be better off getting that spike in your heart.” The sutta goes on in this way, and the images get stronger and stronger."* The five themes — hair of head (kesā), hair of body (lomā), nails (nakhā), teeth (dantā), skin (taco) — are not arbitrary. They target the root of infatuation with the body. The skin, as the outermost layer, is what we are actually attracted to when we conceive of a body as beautiful. Contemplating the skin as a wrapping that holds together otherwise repulsive components directly undercuts sensual desire. This is the very first teaching given to a new monk — showing that the entire path begins with honest, unflinching investigation of the body.
